f1b27e8192:
The guide's wording is short: "window management, drift/bloat prevention (tool-output pruning, compaction), isolation via subagents." Behind it sits most of what makes a long-running agent work or fail.

This chapter treats the context window as a budget you allocate. It shows, with token counts, how agent sessions grow and where the growth comes from. Then it works through every lever, in the order you should reach for them:

  • pruning at the tool;
  • clearing used results, client-side and with the API's clear_tool_uses_20250919 edit;
  • compaction, threshold and on-demand, server-side and client-side;
  • what summarisation loses, and how a persistent case-facts block protects it;
  • placement and the lost-in-the-middle effect;
  • drift detection;
  • sub-agent isolation;
  • scratchpad and state files;
  • retrieval versus stuffing;
  • recovering a session that has degraded.

Two turn-by-turn traces with token counts tie it together.
93466b0289: Reading time: about 2.5 hours  ·  Companion code, 18 runnable examples: ccdvf-companion/16-context-engineering/ (run bash run_all.sh). Everything runs offline, using the shared fake client and ctxlib.py. That's a chars/4 token estimator plus the pairing checks the real API applies.
6560364a79:
Neighbouring chapters: chapter 03 covers memory types, the memory tool, the six-step context ladder at agent level, and the basic shapes of clearing and compaction. This chapter points back to those sections and goes deeper on technique, parameters, cost and failure modes.

Chapter 13 explains tokens and windows from first principles. Chapter 15 prices them and covers prompt caching. Chapter 17 covers prompt wording and placement of instructions. Chapter 21 covers tool design.
0d823e015c:
Every call to Claude is answered from exactly what is in the window on that call, so the quality, cost and latency of an agent are set by what you put there, and in an agent the window fills by itself with tool results the model asked for.

Context engineering is the discipline of keeping that window small, current and well ordered: prune what tools return, clear what has been used, compact what is old while pinning the exact facts a summary would lose, put the important material where the model reads it reliably, and move verbose sub-work and long-lived state out of the window entirely, into sub-agents and files.
5a76f00a09:
At 3.8%, the sub-objective is worth about two direct questions out of 53. But the reasoning runs through agent, cost and tooling questions in other domains as well.

The typical stem describes a symptom that grows with session length. "After about forty tool calls the agent starts re-querying records it already has." "The summary says the customer wants a refund but the amount is gone." "Costs per conversation tripled after we added a log tool." Then it offers four fixes. One is a bigger window or a bigger model. One is a prompt instruction to "remember" or "be concise". One is an arbitrary cap. And one changes what is in the window. The last one is almost always right.

The same reasoning appears in CCAR-F 5.1 and 5.4: progressive summarisation losing numbers, case-facts blocks, scratchpad files, /compact. If you're sitting both exams, this chapter covers those statements too.
ea0d61965a: Context engineering got its name in 2025. But every technique in it has an older ancestor in systems design. Knowing the ancestors helps, because the trade-offs carried over almost unchanged.
43111428ae:
Memory hierarchies and working sets. Peter Denning's working-set model (1968) observed that a program, at any moment, uses a small subset of its pages. Performance collapses ("thrashing") when the resident set is smaller than the working set. The fix wasn't more memory. It was a policy for what stays resident.

An agent's window is the resident set. Tool results it no longer needs are pages that should be evicted. The facts it will need again are the working set, and they must never be evicted. Every clearing and compaction policy in this chapter is an eviction policy.
963cac0b7a:
Caches and write-back. CPU caches and database buffer pools taught the second lesson. Eviction is safe only if what's evicted can be recovered, either because it's still in the backing store or because it was written back.

In context terms, a cleared tool result is safe when the tool can be called again. A compacted conversation is safe only for what was written somewhere else first: a facts block, a state file, a memory file. Information that existed only in the window, and was then summarised away, is a dirty page discarded without write-back.
5d03a0aee7: Retrieval-augmented generation. Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI (2020) paired a retriever with a generator. The model could then answer from documents it was never trained on, by fetching the relevant passages into the prompt per query. The choice between "fetch what this query needs" and "load everything" is section 16 of this chapter. And it's older than LLMs: it's the index-versus-table-scan decision.
b7d1652ca3:
Lost in the middle. Liu and colleagues ("Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts", 2023) measured a U-shaped curve. Models answer more accurately when the relevant passage sits at the beginning or end of a long input than when it sits in the middle.

Models have improved since. Anthropic's own long-context guidance focuses on ordering (long documents first, the question last) rather than on the curve itself. But the placement lesson stands, and the exam uses the phrase (section 12).
aca3b4a983: Virtual context. MemGPT (Packer and colleagues, 2023) framed the window as main memory and external stores as disk. The model paged information in and out through function calls. Anthropic's memory tool (chapter 03) follows the same idea, with plain files.
6c3d6beefe:
The name. In 2025, practitioners started calling the whole practice "context engineering", to set it apart from writing a single good prompt. Anthropic's "Effective context engineering for AI agents" (September 2025) gave the working definition this chapter uses. Find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that makes the desired outcome likely. Treat context as a finite attention budget with diminishing returns.

The same month, the API gained server-side context editing: clearing old tool results and thinking blocks. Server-side compaction followed in two forms, at a threshold (2026-01) and on demand (2026-09). Claude Code had compacted automatically, and offered /compact and /clear, since well before either.
95cbebb7af:
Chapter 13 explained what a token is and why a window has a size. Here the question is operational. What occupies the window on a call? Which of those things do you control? And how much room should you leave?

Everything the model sees on one request counts against one window:

  • the system prompt;
  • the tool definitions (names, descriptions and JSON schemas, plus any system prompt text the API adds for tool use);
  • every message in messages, including tool_use inputs and tool_result contents;
  • images and PDF pages;
  • thinking blocks from earlier turns that the model keeps;
  • the output this call will generate, including any thinking it does now.

Input and output share the window. If you ask for max_tokens of 32,000, those tokens are spoken for even if the model writes 400.
ec0dca5a6f:
At the time of writing, the current models (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.1) all have a 1M-token window by default, with no beta header. They can generate up to 128k output tokens per request. They're billed at standard rates for long prompts, except Haiku 5.5, where prompts over 100,000 tokens cost more. (Check the docs; these numbers move.) Older models such as Sonnet 4.5 have 200k.

A 1M window changes what is possible, not what is wise. A million tokens of input costs a million tokens of input on every turn. It takes longer before the first output token. And it gives the model a million tokens to attend over.

That's why the useful number in production is a working limit you choose. It sits far below the hard limit, and it's the point at which your context policy starts acting.
86c53ac8a4: Write the budget down as line items, exactly as you'd size a JVM heap or a Kafka consumer's memory. Example 01_budget_calculator.py does this for a support agent with a 200,000-token working limit:
202a42711c:
Three things in that table are worth noticing.

First, the fixed lines (system prompt, tool definitions, facts block, retrieval) are small. They're also the lines that matter most per token. The history line is huge, and by the time it's large it's mostly low value.

Second, the output reserve is real. A model running with extended or adaptive thinking may spend most of its max_tokens thinking, and those tokens come out of the same window.

Third, the only line that grows on its own is the history. It grows at a rate you can measure from traces (here 4,200 tokens per tool turn). Divide the free space by the growth rate, and you know how many turns the agent gets before something must happen. That number is the design input for every technique later in the chapter.
f62404c243:
Know the overflow behaviour precisely, because a stem may describe it.

If the input alone exceeds the window, the API returns a 400 invalid_request_error ("prompt is too long") on every model.

If the input fits but input plus max_tokens exceeds the window, it depends on the model. Models from the Claude 4.5 generation onward accept the request. If generation actually reaches the limit, they stop with stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded". Earlier models rejected such requests up front, unless you opted in with a beta header (check the docs).

So a long-running agent on a current model can get a 200 whose stop reason means "I ran out of window mid-answer". The loop must treat it like max_tokens, plus a signal that the history needs work. Compact or restart from state, then continue (example 17).
f1164310b3:
Some models also know their budget. Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5 receive automatic "context awareness". The API injects the total budget into the system prompt, and adds a <system_warning> with usage and remaining tokens after each tool call. That lets the model pace itself.

Opus 4.7 and later, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable don't receive these tags. For them, a beta "task budgets" feature lets you set an explicit budget (check the docs for both).

For the exam, the point is this. The model's awareness of its budget depends on the model. Your harness's awareness is always your job.
5654bc263c:
Estimating with characters divided by four is fine for design, and the companion does it. Production code should count.

The token counting endpoint (client.messages.count_tokens) takes the same model, system, tools and messages as a real call. It returns input_tokens without generating anything.

With context editing enabled, the beta counting call also accepts context_management. It reports both the post-edit input_tokens and context_management.original_input_tokens. So you can see what the server's edits would remove before you rely on them. A preflight check turns those numbers into a decision:
fca7b9838e:
Counting costs a round trip, so most harnesses don't count every turn. There's a cheaper pattern. Read usage.input_tokens from the previous response, plus the cache read and cache creation tokens, which are also input. Add an estimate for what you're about to append. Count exactly only when the estimate is within, say, 10% of the working limit.

In Java, the same check is a method on whatever bean builds your requests. If you already have a Micrometer gauge for heap usage, add one for "input tokens at last call" per session, and alert on it the same way.
7d300fea7e: A larger window looks like a free upgrade. So be exact about why "just send everything" fails. There are four separate costs, and they compound.
1c3f2096ca:
Attention is a shared resource. Each output token is produced by attending over every input token, so relevant and irrelevant tokens compete. Anthropic's guidance describes this as context having diminishing returns ("context rot"). As the number of tokens grows, the model's ability to recall and use any specific piece of it degrades. It happens gradually, not at a cliff.

A specific failure follows. A value the agent needs (an order id, a constraint the user stated) is present in the window, but isn't used. Forty thousand tokens of log output sit between it and the current turn.
8b80448747:
Cost is resent. The Messages API is stateless. In a loop, the whole history goes out on every turn. So a tool result added at turn 3 is paid for on every turn after it.

If each turn adds a roughly constant amount r, turn n costs about n·r input tokens. A run of N turns costs about r·N²/2. That quadratic is the arithmetic behind section 05's trace.

Prompt caching (chapter 15) cuts the price of the resent prefix to a tenth, but only while the prefix is unchanged. Context edits change it (section 08).
0e5e5a6e41: Latency follows input. Time to first token grows with input length, and every turn of an agent waits on it. An agent at 150,000 tokens of history is slower on every step than the same agent at 15,000, caching or not.
e6885234b0: The window is finite. Eventually the run hits the hard limit, or more often your working limit, and something has to give. If nothing was designed to give, the run is what gives.
ba2de8fb66: These costs explain why the exam treats "use the model with the larger window" as a distractor whenever the stem describes accumulation. A bigger window postpones the hard failure. It leaves the other three costs in place, or makes them worse.
396f5c451b: The objective names two failure modes: drift and bloat. Practitioners and Anthropic's own write-ups use a few more. Separating them helps you pick the fix, because each has a different cause.
a2a88e9f19:
Abstract arguments about growth are easy to agree with and easy to underestimate. Example 02_growth_trace.py runs one twelve-step support investigation twice, with identical tool calls. A customer, C-7781, says order O-55120 never arrived.

The agent looks up the account, lists orders, and reads the order. It searches the knowledge base, reads the refund policy, and checks the shipment. It searches carrier logs, reads the invoice, and searches the knowledge base again. Then it reads the credit rules, calculates a credit and opens a case.

The system prompt is about 2,000 tokens. Six tool definitions add about 1,800.
bfc1398e9a:
The unmanaged run returns raw tool payloads and keeps everything. The managed run applies three changes:

  • tools return projections, the fields the next decision needs;
  • results older than the three most recent tool uses are replaced by a placeholder;
  • the policy document is excluded from clearing, because the agent must keep consulting it.

Here is the trace:
41688670ba:
The unmanaged per-turn column only goes up. Every tool result is still there at turn 12. That includes the 20,000-token log search from turn 7, whose only useful content was one line. By turn 12 the request is 76,000 tokens. Perhaps 4,000 of those are relevant to "open the case with the right credit".

The cumulative column is what you pay. It reaches 562,000 tokens of input for a twelve-step task. That's the quadratic from section 04, made visible.
56c1d5515c:
The managed per-turn column plateaus. After turn 5 it hovers around 11,000 tokens. Each new result is small, and old ones are cleared as new ones arrive.

The step at turn 5 is the policy document (6,000 tokens), which is deliberately excluded from clearing. That's a cost you choose to pay, because the agent needs the policy until the end.

A plateau is the shape you want. Per-turn cost becomes roughly constant, so total cost grows linearly with the number of turns, not quadratically.
b47fa7b5e5:
Where the 80% came from. Roughly two thirds of the saving is pruning at the tool. Turn 2's order list is 600 tokens instead of 9,000. Turn 7's log search is 700 instead of 20,000. The other third is clearing.

That ratio is typical. It's why the ladder in chapter 03 puts pruning before clearing. The cheapest token is the one that never enters the window. And pruning also removes noise from the turn where the result is first read, which clearing can't do.
55bc08bbd7:
What the managed run gave up. At turn 12, the managed agent can no longer see the raw order list or the log lines. If it needs them, it must call the tool again.

That's the bargain. It's a good one when tools are cheap and idempotent. It's a bad one for a tool that's slow, rate-limited or non-deterministic, like a web search whose results change. That case is what exclude_tools and a facts block are for.
0f477fd9b3:
Most bloat in an agent comes from tools, and you write the tools.

A tool written for a human dashboard, or for another service, returns everything it has. A human can scroll, and a service can ignore fields. A tool written for a model should return what the next decision needs, a count of what else exists, and a way to get more.

The model can't ignore fields. Everything you return is read, paid for on every later turn, and competes for attention.
2d8a92381f: Example 03_tool_output_pruning.py shows the difference on an order search over 200 orders. Each order has line items, an audit block and a billing address.
61e6d8c151:
Each element of the fixed version does a specific job.

  • Filter parameters (status) let the model ask a narrower question. Otherwise it receives everything and filters in its head, which it does less reliably than a WHERE clause.
  • Projection returns the five fields that decide what to do next. Detail stays one call away.
  • Pagination with a total tells the model that 66 lost orders exist and it has seen ten. That prevents a silent failure, where the model concludes from a truncated list that an order doesn't exist.
  • The note names the follow-up tool. It's a cheap way to steer the next call.

The ratio here is 98 to 1. Ratios of 10 to 100 are normal for list-shaped tools.
a4834debb2: Logs and documents need a different shape. Their value is in a few lines scattered through many. Example 04_log_pruner.py turns an hour of eNodeB log, 4,157 lines and about 31,000 tokens, into this:
0317b1a1ae:
The pruner does four things, in order:

  1. severity filtering: drop INFO and DEBUG;
  2. normalisation: mask the varying number in count=3, so repeated messages collapse;
  3. deduplication, with counts and first-seen time;
  4. a header that states what was suppressed.

The header matters more than it looks. Without it, the model sees two lines and may conclude the hour was quiet apart from them. With it, the model knows 4,115 lines were dropped by rule. It can ask for a time slice if it needs context around 02:41.

Truncation without a marker is one of the anti-patterns in section 19. A file read that silently stops at 2,000 lines invites the model to reason about a function whose second half it never saw.
27fe218f8d: In a Spring service, the natural place for projection is a response record per tool, separate from your domain entity. It's exactly how you separate a public DTO from a JPA entity. It also gives you a unit-testable contract for "what the model sees".
56291d0de7:
Pruning at the tool makes each result small. It doesn't stop small results from piling up. And some results are unavoidably large, like a policy document or a source file under edit. The next step is to remove results from the history once they've been used.

Chapter 03 section 11 showed the basic broken and fixed versions. In short: never delete a tool_result block. The API rejects any history in which an assistant tool_use id has no matching result in the next user turn. Instead, replace the content of old results with a short placeholder, and keep every block and id.

This section is about the decisions inside that policy. The exam, and real incidents, are about the decisions.
b85d2add9f:
Which results to clear. Oldest first is the default, because the most recent results are the ones the model is still reasoning about.

Count-based retention ("keep the last three tool uses") is simple and predictable. Token-based retention ("keep results until the history is under 30,000 tokens") adapts to result size. But it makes the cut point jump around, which hurts caching. A hybrid many teams use: keep the last N, and also clear any single result larger than a threshold once it's two turns old.
aaf90be0be:
What never to clear. Results the agent needs to keep consulting:

  • a policy document it must check every refund against;
  • the file it's currently editing;
  • memory-tool reads;
  • results from tools that are expensive or non-deterministic to call again (web search, a slow mainframe query, a paid data API).

These go on an exclusion list. If a large result must stay, ask whether it belongs in the system prompt or a facts block instead. There it's stable and cacheable.
13eb6af67a: What the placeholder says. "[cleared]" is legal. "[tool result cleared after use; call get_order again if you need it]" is better. It tells the model the information existed, and how to get it back. Without that, a model that sees a gap may assume the call failed and retry immediately. Or, worse, it may assume the result was empty.
a69d8c37a3: Whether to clear inputs too. Tool inputs are usually small. Occasionally they aren't, as with a write_file call whose input is the whole file. Then clearing them saves as much as clearing the result. The cost is that the model can no longer see what it asked for. That matters if it's about to ask again.
4473fbc308:
Thinking blocks. Say you use extended or adaptive thinking with tools. When you post the tool result, the API requires the thinking block that preceded the tool_use to be sent back unmodified, with its signature. So client-side edits must never rewrite or reorder thinking blocks in the current tool cycle.

On the 5.5-generation models, editing earlier turns client-side can also invalidate thinking blocks in every later assistant turn. New accounts from 31 August 2026 get a rejection, not a silent drop, when an invalidated block is replayed (check the docs, "keeping the prefix unchanged").

This is one of the strongest practical reasons to let the server do the editing (section 08). Server-side context management never invalidates thinking blocks on those models.
50eba9e2bd: Keep your stored history complete, even when you send a cleared copy. Clearing is a view over the log, not a mutation of it. The full transcript is your audit trail and your replay fixture (chapter 12). It's also your evidence when a customer disputes what the agent said. In Spring terms, the conversation table is append-only, and the "request builder" produces a projection of it per call.
